result.text: The paper addresses constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) in continuous state-action spaces, aiming to maximize long-term reward while satisfying safety or resource constraints with zero violation. Its key insight is to combine a conservative update scheme with natural policy gradient in a primal-dual framework, which stabilizes dual iterates and enforces constraints more strictly so that violations vanish in the limit. The proposed Conservative Natural Policy Gradient Primal-Dual (CNPGPD) algorithm uses natural-gradient policy updates together with a conservative adjustment to the dual variables and policy class restriction to guarantee convergence of the value function to the global optimum up to approximation error from parametrization, while improving sample complexity over prior constrained NPGPD methods. Empirical results corroborate that CNPGPD attains state-of-the-art objective performance while achieving zero constraint violation for infinite-horizon discounted CMDPs.

The paper tackles the limitation of contrastive image-text pre-training (e.g., CLIP) that treats examples as independent pairs and thus overlooks richer semantic relationships across modalities. Its key insight is that injecting structured semantic knowledge from knowledge graphs into the pre-training objective will force vision and language representations to align not only at the instance level but also along concept-level relations, improving cross-modal semantic consistency and reasoning. The method, Knowledge-CLIP, augments CLIP by creating knowledge-graph-derived training tuples (nodes, edges, and multi-hop relations) and adding knowledge-based objectives alongside the standard contrastive loss so that images, captions, and concept nodes are jointly embedded and encouraged to respect graph structure; experiments show gains on a variety of vision–language tasks over CLIP and other baselines.

The paper tackles the limitation of current Tree-of-Thought and related methods that rely on pre-trained LLMs as value functions and thus struggle in domains lacking model knowledge or requiring long-horizon planning. Its key insight is that an AlphaZero-style tree search combined with a learned value function can robustly guide LLM decoding and be applied across tasks and model sizes, rather than depending on the frozen pre-trained model for evaluation. The proposed TS-LLM framework trains a value and policy model alongside tree search to perform Monte Carlo-style planning during both inference and training, iteratively improving the LLM’s outputs. Experiments on reasoning, planning, alignment, and decision-making tasks demonstrate that TS-LLM outperforms prior approaches and scales to deep search trees (up to depth 64).

MultiDiffusion addresses the problem of adding versatile, user-specified control to pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models without expensive retraining or task-specific hacks. The key insight is to cast controlled generation as an optimization that ties together multiple diffusion sampling processes via shared parameters or constraints, effectively fusing their denoising paths so the model jointly respects diverse constraints. Practically, the method runs several coupled diffusion processes (e.g., different crops, aspect ratios, or spatial conditioning channels) and enforces consistency through an objective that coordinates their latent updates, enabling high-quality, diverse outputs that obey controls like panoramas, segmentation masks, or bounding boxes using only a pretrained model.

The paper addresses continuous super-resolution of screen content images (SCIs), which differ from natural images and must be upscaled to arbitrary scales after aggressive downsampling and compression for bandwidth savings. The key insight is to treat SR as an implicit coordinate-to-pixel prediction problem where query pixel values can be inferred from learned feature "keys" via an implicit transformer that aggregates information from similar neighboring pixels using an implicit position encoding. The proposed Implicit Transformer Super-Resolution Network (ITSRN) extracts image features at key coordinates and uses the implicit transformer plus position encoding to produce high-quality continuous SR at arbitrary ratios. They validate ITSRN on newly constructed SCI1K and SCI1K-compression benchmarks, showing substantial improvements over existing continuous and discrete SR methods on both compressed and uncompressed SCIs.

The paper tackles expressive human pose and shape estimation (EHPS), aiming to robustly recover full-body, hand, and face motion across diverse scenes where prior methods are limited by small, narrow datasets and modest model capacity. The key insight is that scaling both data—curating and training on a large, heterogeneous pool of 4.5M annotated instances from 32 EHPS datasets selected via systematic benchmarking—and model size—using large vision transformers up to ViT-Huge—yields a generalist foundation model whose representations transfer broadly and set new state-of-the-art results. Methodologically, the authors build SMPLer-X by (1) performing extensive dataset benchmarking to choose complementary training sources and optimize the training scheme, (2) training large ViT-based models on the aggregated data, and (3) applying finetuning strategies to convert the foundation model into high-performing specialist variants, demonstrating strong zero-shot and finetuned performance across multiple benchmarks.

The paper tackles the mismatch between pruning objectives (minimizing remaining weights) and actual inference time, aiming to produce pruned DNNs that meet a user-specified speedup on a target system while minimizing accuracy loss. The key insight is to frame pruning as a speedup-constrained layer-wise allocation problem—optimal layer sparsities should be chosen with knowledge of both layer sensitivity and the real runtime cost on the hardware, rather than by simply reducing parameter count. SPDY implements this by combining an efficient dynamic programming solver that finds layer-wise sparsities that satisfy a desired speedup given sensitivity scores, with a local search procedure that estimates accurate per-layer sensitivity scores; the pipeline is compatible with one-shot and gradual pruning and extends to low-data and structured patterns (e.g., GPU 2:4) to empirically deliver guaranteed speedups with improved accuracy recovery.

The paper addresses the lack of realistic convergence guarantees for Plug-and-Play (PnP) image restoration methods, which use learned denoisers as priors but often rely on restrictive assumptions or convex data terms. The key insight is to design the denoiser as a single gradient descent step on a learned functional, so that the overall scheme can be interpreted as a proximal-gradient solver for an explicit global objective; this lets the authors leverage nonconvex proximal-gradient convergence theory to ensure the iterates approach stationary points. Methodologically, they embed this "gradient-step denoiser" into a half-quadratic splitting PnP framework, train the neural-network-parameterized functional to act as a high-quality denoiser, and demonstrate empirically on deblurring, super-resolution and inpainting that the algorithm converges in practice and achieves state-of-the-art restoration performance.

The paper addresses domain shift in classification, especially settings that are anti-causal (labels Y cause covariates X) where conventional approaches that seek predictors based only on Y’s causal parents fail because Y has no parents. The key insight is that even under anti-causal structure there exists shared causal structure across domains that can be exploited by disentangling features into invariant components (stable across domains) and non-stable components (domain-specific) so as to admit an invariant predictor while enabling rapid adaptation. Methodologically, the authors formalize a notion of domain shift consistent with causal invariance, derive learning principles that separate invariant and non-stable features, and implement a representation-learning algorithm that enforces this decomposition to produce transportable representations; empirical results on synthetic and real data validate improved robustness and fast adaptation.

The paper tackles the problem of building allocentric top-down semantic maps from egocentric RGB-D tours so an embodied agent can form persistent spatio-semantic memories for downstream tasks like object navigation and question answering. Its key insight is to combine geometric projection from egocentric views with learned neural spatial memory so the system both grounds features in metric floor-plan coordinates and accumulates them over time into a rich allocentric representation. The proposed Semantic MapNet (SMNet) implements this by encoding each RGB-D frame with an egocentric visual encoder, projecting those features into floor-plan locations via a feature projector, accumulating them in a learned spatial memory tensor (width×length×channels), and decoding that tensor into top-down semantic maps; this hybrid geometry-plus-learning approach yields large gains on Matterport3D semantic mapping and produces representations usable for ObjectNav and Embodied QA.

The proposed Conservative Natural Policy Gradient Primal-Dual (CNPGPD) algorithm uses natural-gradient policy updates together with a conservative adjustment to the dual variables and policy class restriction to guarantee convergence of the value function to the global optimum up to approximation error from parametrization, while improving sample complexity over prior constrained NPGPD methods. Empirical results corroborate that CNPGPD attains state-of-the-art objective performance while achieving zero constraint violation for infinite-horizon discounted CMDPs.

The key insight is that allowing small constraint violations makes CMDP learning no harder than unconstrained MDPs (same dependence on state, action, discount, and accuracy), while enforcing strict feasibility fundamentally increases difficulty by a factor depending on the Slater constant that measures margin in the feasible set. Methodologically, the authors design a model-based algorithm that estimates transition dynamics and solves a constrained optimization (with different treatments for relaxed vs. strict feasibility), and they prove upper bounds of Õ(SA(1−γ)^{-3}ε^{-2}) for relaxed feasibility and Õ(SA(1−γ)^{-5}ε^{-2}ζ^{-2}) for strict feasibility, together with a matching lower bound for the strict case, yielding near-minimax optimal guarantees.

result.text: The paper tackles the scalability and complexity limitations of vision-language pretraining, where prior methods rely on expensive clean captions, region labels, and multiple dataset-specific objectives. Its key insight is that large-scale weakly supervised image–text pairs and a single unified pretraining objective—prefix language modeling—are sufficient to learn strong multimodal representations without task-specific losses or heavy annotation. The method, SimVLM, trains an end-to-end encoder–decoder Transformer on massive noisy web-scraped image–text data using only the prefix LM objective to predict text conditioned on visual input, and then fine-tunes or evaluates the model on diverse downstream tasks. This simple approach yields state-of-the-art results across discriminative and generative benchmarks and demonstrates strong zero-shot and transfer capabilities.

The key insight is that treating an image as a sequence of flattened fixed-size patches (e.g., 16x16) and feeding these patch embeddings directly to a standard Transformer yields strong visual representations when trained at scale. The method constructs a Vision Transformer (ViT) that splits images into non-overlapping patches, linearly projects them to tokens, adds positional embeddings and a classification token, and then applies the Transformer encoder; when pre-trained on very large datasets and fine-tuned on downstream vision benchmarks, ViT matches or exceeds state-of-the-art CNNs while being more compute-efficient in training.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of achieving full fine-tuning (FFT) accuracy for large language models under tight computational and memory constraints by improving parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). Its key insight is that model updates can be decomposed into a jointly trained low-rank component and a highly sparse component—drawing on robust PCA ideas—so that their combination more faithfully approximates FFT than either low-rank or sparse updates alone. result.text: This paper addresses the lack of theoretical recovery guarantees for plug-and-play (PnP) and regularization by denoising (RED) methods used to solve inverse problems with pre-trained deep denoisers as priors. The key insight is that poor gradient flow at initialization is a primary cause of failure for static sparse networks, DST improves performance by dynamically improving gradient flow during training, and LTs succeed not by better gradient flow but by re-learning a previously found pruning solution. Its key insight is that combining optimism for reward with pessimism for constraints—leveraging a known strictly safe baseline when available or conservatively estimating constraint costs otherwise—lets an agent explore without incurring growing safety breaches. result.text: The paper addresses improving decision-making under uncertainty using large language models (LLMs), noting that naive prompting performs poorly as problem complexity grows. The key insight is that integrating decision- and utility-theoretic principles with modern multi-step, scalable inference-time reasoning yields more accurate and auditable decisions than one-shot prompts. The proposed DeLLMa framework implements a structured, multi-step reasoning pipeline that decomposes problems, elicits and weighs probabilistic beliefs and utilities, and aggregates simulated or sampled outcomes to select high-utility actions. Empirical validation across realistic decision environments shows consistent improvements—up to 40% higher accuracy over baselines—and demonstrates further gains from scaling compute at test time, supported by human evaluations of component effectiveness.

result.text: The paper addresses blind image super-resolution where the low-resolution inputs have unknown, complex degradations (blur, noise, JPEG, etc.) and explicit per-degradation estimators are impractical or non-generalizable. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of efficient object-goal navigation in novel, visually realistic environments by learning semantic cues and layout regularities without access to action or goal labels, using only passive YouTube video data. The key insight is that off-policy Q-learning can be applied to pseudo-labeled transition quadruples (image, action, next image, reward) extracted from unannotated videos to discover useful semantic affordances and spatial priors for navigation despite suboptimal or unlabeled behavior. The method constructs approximate action and reward labels from video frame transitions, trains Q-functions on these passive transitions, and incorporates the learned semantic cues into a hierarchical navigation policy that selects subgoals and low-level controls. This approach yields much more efficient object-goal navigation in simulation—improving over end-to-end RL by 66% while requiring roughly 250× fewer environment interactions.

The key insight is that a modular algorithmic framework can handle both smooth concave reward with convex constraints and hard knapsack-style constraints while admitting strong theoretical guarantees. The method combines tabular episodic RL with a modular primal–dual style treatment of constraints—using concave-convex optimization tools for the smooth case and resource accounting/consumption bookkeeping for knapsacks—yielding regret and constraint-violation bounds that improve on existing approaches. result.text: The paper addresses the performance gap between low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and full fine-tuning of foundation models, asking whether LoRA is being properly optimized. The key insight is that LoRA-based optimization is mathematically equivalent to full fine-tuning with a low-rank gradient, and that this low-rank gradient can be expressed directly from the gradients of LoRA’s two low-rank matrices; therefore, improving LoRA amounts to better approximating the full-fine-tuning gradient via adjustments to those matrix gradients. The authors propose LoRA-Pro, which derives and applies theoretically optimal adjustments to the low-rank matrix gradients so the resulting low-rank update more closely matches the full fine-tuning gradient, and they validate this approach across diverse tasks—showing substantial closing of the performance gap.

The proposed method, Continuous Doubly Constrained Batch RL, implements these two simple penalties—one that penalizes policy deviation from the behavior policy and another that regularizes value estimates toward conservative targets—within a standard actor-critic framework to train policies without online interaction. result.text: The paper addresses sample-efficient learning in episodic finite-horizon constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), where an agent must minimize a primary cost while satisfying one or more constraint costs, all within a fixed episode length. The method is an online algorithm that constructs confidence sets for transitions, performs optimistic planning via solving the CMDP LP in each episode to pick exploratory policies, and is shown to require a number of episodes that scales linearly with |S||A| and quadratically with the horizon H and the maximum number of possible successors per state-action, yielding particularly favorable sample complexity when that successor bound is much smaller than |S|.

The authors introduce GITA, an end-to-end framework that converts graph data into aligned visual and textual inputs, augments visual layouts, and trains multimodal fusion models, and they construct the GVLQA benchmark (a vision-language question answering dataset derived from existing graph datasets) to pretrain and evaluate the approach. Experiments on GVLQA and five real-world datasets show GITA outperforms mainstream LLM baselines, with ablations highlighting the benefits of layout augmentation and pretraining on the visual-graph dataset.

The key insight is that many hard language-modeling steps contain easier subtasks that smaller, faster models can approximate well, and that speculative execution combined with a corrective sampling test can let a large model validate and accept multiple tokens proposed by the small model without changing the overall output distribution. Their method, speculative decoding, runs a cheap proposal model to generate several token candidates in parallel, then runs the expensive target model in parallel to accept or reject those tokens via a novel sampling/correction procedure that preserves exact sampling from the original model. result.text: The paper studies why invariance-based causal methods like invariant risk minimization (IRM) often fail at out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization for classification, asking whether the problem is method failure or a limitation of the invariance principle itself. result.text: The paper studies why low-rank adaptation (LoRA) works for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models by analyzing training dynamics in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime and asking whether LoRA introduces optimization issues. The key insight is that full fine-tuning already admits a good low-rank solution of rank r ≲ √N for N data points, and choosing a LoRA rank r ≳ √N matches this capacity so that the restricted optimization landscape has no spurious local minima. Concretely, the authors prove that with LoRA of sufficient rank gradient descent provably converges to these low-rank solutions in the NTK limit, and they additionally show that the recovered low-rank solutions generalize well to new data.

result.text: The paper addresses the computational bottleneck of Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models, whose self-attention layers incur quadratic cost and slow high-resolution image and video generation. The key insight is that DiT inference exhibits three kinds of redundancy—spatial (many heads attend locally), temporal (neighboring timesteps produce similar attention outputs), and conditional (conditional and unconditional passes are similar)—which can be exploited post-training to avoid repeated costly attention computations. The method, DiTFastAttn, implements three complementary compression techniques: Window Attention with Residual Sharing to localize and reuse spatial attention computation, Attention Sharing across Timesteps to reuse attention maps between nearby diffusion steps, and Attention Sharing across Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) to skip redundant conditional/unconditional attention work; applied to DiT, PixArt-Sigma, and OpenSora, this yields up to 76% reduction in attention FLOPs and up to 1.8× end-to-end speedup for high-resolution generation.

result.text: The paper tackles safe offline reinforcement learning, where enforcing zero safety violations is critical but difficult because it requires balancing safety, reward maximization, and staying close to offline data. The key insight is that hard safety constraints can be reformulated via reachability analysis as identifying the largest feasible region supported by the dataset, turning the original tri-objective into a feasibility-dependent objective that maximizes reward inside the feasible region and minimizes risk outside it. Building on this, the authors propose FISOR (FeasIbility-guided Safe Offline RL), which decouples constraint adherence, reward optimization, and behavior regularization into three processes and shows the optimal policy takes the form of a weighted behavior cloning solution. To extract that policy efficiently they introduce an energy-guided diffusion model that avoids training a time-dependent classifier, simplifying training while empirically ensuring zero violations across tasks and achieving top returns on the DSRL benchmark.

result.text: The paper addresses the lack of realistic convergence guarantees for Plug-and-Play (PnP) image restoration methods, which use learned denoisers as priors but often rely on restrictive assumptions or convex data terms. result.text: The paper tackles slow speculative decoding for LLM inference, where a smaller draft model currently generates tokens autoregressively and spends equal time on all tokens, causing inefficiencies and limited speedups. The key insight is that removing autoregressive drafting and reallocating drafting effort non-uniformly across tokens can greatly reduce wasted computation while still preserving the target model’s output distribution. The proposed Cascade Speculative Drafting (CS Drafting) introduces a Vertical Cascade that replaces neural autoregressive token-by-token generation with parallel or non-autoregressive drafting, and a Horizontal Cascade that dynamically prioritizes and allocates drafting time to more important or uncertain tokens; combined, these cascades let the target model accept larger portions of drafts less frequently and thus run fewer iterations. args.text: Quantile-Adaptive Modular Adaptation (QAMA): learn a representation that decomposes into an invariant backbone (regularized by an information bottleneck) and K domain-specific mechanisms, each equipped with a tiny adapter (e.g., BN affine or low-rank update). During training, we simulate sparse mechanism shifts across held-out domains and meta-optimize the post-adaptation α-quantile of the risk, so the model learns to quickly identify and update only the shifted mechanisms from a few unlabeled samples via a self-supervised probe. At test time, we adapt just those adapters (and optionally query a handful of labels if budgeted) while freezing the invariant backbone, yielding robustness without discarding predictive domain-specific signal. Under s-sparse shifts (s ≪ K), this design reduces worst-α risk and adaptation sample complexity compared to static invariance or mean-risk adaptation, unifying disentanglement, quantile risk, and parameter-efficient TTA.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding why Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is so effective for parameter-efficient fine-tuning by formally analyzing its expressive power: specifically, what class of target models can be represented by adding low-rank adapters to a pre-trained network. The key insight is that LoRA’s capacity is governed by a simple rank threshold that depends on the source model’s width and the relative depths of source and target networks, and that sufficiently large but still low-rank adapters suffice to emulate smaller target models exactly. Methodologically, the authors prove constructive representation theorems for fully connected networks—showing LoRA can adapt any model f to any smaller target \overline{f} when LoRA rank ≥ (width of f) × (depth of \overline{f} / depth of f) and provide bounds on approximation error below this threshold—and extend the analysis to Transformers, proving rank-(embedding size/2) adapters can realize any same-size target model.

result.text: The paper tackles the mismatch in Plug-and-Play (PnP) image restoration where denoisers are applied to progressively less noisy intermediate images, unlike diffusion-based methods that denoise re-noised inputs, potentially degrading regularization. The key insight is that overfitting a small multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to map continuous pixel coordinates to RGB values produces a compact, continuous representation whose learned weights encode the image and can be quantized to form a compressed code; this implicit neural representation can outperform JPEG at low bitrates even without entropy coding. We cast adapter configuration as a speedup-constrained allocation with device-measured per-layer cost models, solving a knapsack-like objective over discrete ranks and sparsity patterns using dynamic programming to maximize an accuracy proxy under the hardware budget. During training, we use a RoSA-style low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition with hardware-friendly sparsity, apply LoRA-Pro-inspired gradient corrections to better match the full fine-tuning gradient, and periodically resample low-rank projections as in Flora to realize higher effective rank without extra optimizer state. result.text: The paper studies fundamental limits of offline reinforcement learning with linear function approximation, asking what representational and distributional conditions are necessary for sample-efficient offline policy evaluation. Its key insight is a negative one: even with strong realizability (every policy's value function is exactly linear in given features) and strong coverage of the offline data (a spectral condition on features), any algorithm still requires a number of offline samples exponential in the horizon to nontrivially estimate a policy's value. The authors establish this by constructing hard MDP families and proving information-theoretic lower bounds that rule out sub-exponential sample complexity under those assumptions, and they identify the only ways to evade the lower bound as imposing much stronger conditions such as low distribution shift between offline data and the target policy or substantially richer representation beyond mere realizability.

args.text: Consensus-Control Diffusion: a training-free mechanism that, at each denoising step, unrolls a few iterations of a small consensus optimization (ADMM-style) to reconcile the base denoiser with multiple heterogeneous controls (edges/depth/segmentation/color/flow/text regions). Each control contributes either a differentiable guidance loss (e.g., optical-flow or mask consistency) or a latent proposal from a lightweight adapter; the consensus update blends these via spatially varying weights estimated from per-control uncertainty derived from score variance between conditional/unconditional and a degraded "bad-guide" ensemble. This yields per-pixel, per-timestep allocation of a control budget—structure-heavy pixels lean on visual controls while style/background lean on text—while multi-crop/tiling proposals are fused in the same consensus to support large canvases. The approach preserves diversity relative to strong CFG, improves constraint satisfaction over naive guidance, and remains modular and composable across new control types without retraining.

result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency in speculative decoding for accelerating large language model inference, where a fast draft model proposes token blocks that a target model must verify to ensure lossless sampling. The key insight is that verifying an entire drafted block jointly—rather than checking tokens independently—yields strictly better or equal expected progress per iteration and can reduce wall-clock time without sacrificing the exact-sample guarantee. The authors introduce Block Verification, a simple algorithm for joint block verification, prove its optimality in expected tokens produced per iteration relative to token-level checks, and empirically show consistent 5–8% speedups across tasks and datasets. Because it preserves correctness, adds no implementation complexity, and never worsens performance, block verification is recommended as a default refinement for speculative decoding.

args.text: We propose Score-Projection Composable Control, a training-free sampler that fuses many control signals (edges, depth, segmentation, flow, boxes) by projecting the diffusion score at each step onto a consensus direction that jointly reduces all control losses. Concretely, for any differentiable control encoder we compute its loss gradient with respect to the current denoised latent and solve a small weighted least-squares trust-region problem to find the minimum-norm adjustment to the model score, effectively unifying MultiDiffusion-style constraint coupling with gradient-based guidance. To keep it fast and precise, we cache and share Jacobian–vector products across neighboring timesteps and apply spatial gating via DiffEdit-like automatic masks, while remaining plug-and-play with adapter/control encoders from T2I-Adapter and Uni-ControlNet. This single-trajectory projection yields stronger multi-control satisfaction and better image fidelity than independent adapters or single-control guidance, while preserving diversity and extending naturally to dense motion and panorama/layout constraints.

result.text: Hardware-Aware Robust PEFT proposes jointly selecting per-layer low-rank adapter ranks and structured sparse adapter masks (e.g., n:m patterns like 2:4) to meet a specified latency or energy target on a given accelerator while minimizing the gap to full fine-tuning. We cast adapter configuration as a speedup-constrained allocation with device-measured per-layer cost models, solving a knapsack-like objective over discrete ranks and sparsity patterns using dynamic programming to maximize an accuracy proxy under the hardware budget. During training, we use a RoSA-style low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition with hardware-friendly sparsity, apply LoRA-Pro-inspired gradient corrections to better match the full fine-tuning gradient, and periodically resample low-rank projections as in Flora to realize higher effective rank without extra optimizer state. This yields PEFT configurations with predictable on-device speedups and strong accuracy, enabled by sparse kernels tuned to the chosen structured patterns.

result.text: Ctrl-X tackles the problem of providing fast, flexible structure and appearance control for text-to-image diffusion models without adding extra training or iterative guidance, overcoming the slow per-sample latent optimization used by prior methods. Methodologically, Ctrl-X injects a structure image condition into the diffusion model through a designed feed-forward pathway to align spatial layout, and applies a semantic-aware appearance transfer module to map appearance from an arbitrary input image onto the generated content, enabling plug-and-play use with existing T2I and T2V checkpoints and delivering faster, higher-quality control across varied condition modalities.

args.text: We propose a scale-conditioned, degradation-aware implicit video super-resolution model tailored for screen-content videos with unknown compression artifacts and arbitrary (including non-integer/asymmetric) scales. Per-frame reconstruction is performed by an implicit transformer that predicts high-resolution pixels from coordinate queries augmented with Fourier feature encodings and explicit scale tokens, while temporal fusion uses SAVSR-style omni-dimensional scale-attention to adapt inter-frame feature extraction and upsampling. A knowledge-distilled implicit degradation representation, learned from paired HR–LR patches, conditions both feature alignment and the implicit aggregator to perform targeted deblocking/deringing without oversmoothing sharp text and GUI edges. This single model unifies arbitrary-scale VSR and blind artifact handling, improving fidelity and readability over frame-wise implicit SR and fixed-scale VSR baselines on screen-content video benchmarks.

args.text: We propose Speculative Tree Search for LLMs (STS-LLM): integrate AlphaZero-style learned-value tree search with lossless speculative drafting to amortize expansion and rollout costs across deep search. A small draft policy conditioned on tree state proposes multi-token thought continuations for many frontier nodes in parallel; the target model then performs joint block verification to accept long prefixes and only computes policy/value at verified anchors, while a horizontal cascade allocates drafting budget to high-uncertainty nodes. Because verification preserves the target model’s induced distribution, STS-LLM maintains search equivalence to the non-speculative baseline but achieves far fewer target-model passes per expanded edge, enabling deeper/wider trees under the same compute budget. We hypothesize Pareto improvements over vanilla TS-LLM and over standard speculative decoding in long-horizon math/planning, and outline an evaluation that fixes target-model FLOPs to compare achieved tree depth, effective branching factor, and final accuracy.

result.text: MultiDiffusion addresses the problem of adding versatile, user-specified control to pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models without expensive retraining or task-specific hacks. The key insight is to cast controlled generation as an optimization that ties together multiple diffusion sampling processes via shared parameters or constraints, effectively fusing their denoising paths so the model jointly respects diverse constraints. Practically, the method runs several coupled diffusion processes (e.g., different crops, aspect ratios, or spatial conditioning channels) and enforces consistency through an objective that coordinates their latent updates, enabling high-quality, diverse outputs that obey controls like panoramas, segmentation masks, or bounding boxes using only a pretrained model.

args.text: We propose Quantile Adaptive Risk Minimization (Q-ARM): train models for high-probability post-adaptation performance by minimizing an α-quantile (or a smooth CVaR surrogate) of the risk after a fixed unsupervised test-time adaptation procedure executed on held-out source domains. Unlike ARM, which optimizes expected post-adaptation risk, Q-ARM concentrates learning on the heavy tail of domain shifts, yielding adaptation rules that are robust to rare but severe shifts without the over-conservatism of worst-case training. The objective differentiates through the adaptation steps and aggregates per-domain post-adaptation losses via a quantile/CVaR operator; theoretically, under i.i.d. domains from a meta-distribution, Q-ARM inherits generalization guarantees analogous to QRM and recovers causal/invariant predictors as α→1 while still permitting rapid adaptation. Empirically, we expect Q-ARM to close the gap between average-case robust adaptation and worst-case DG by prioritizing challenging domains during meta-training.

args.text: ControlRouter is a training-free arbitration plugin for composable multi-modal control in text-to-image diffusion. The resulting weights gate adapter/ControlNet injections and are temporally smoothed across steps, while a MultiDiffusion-style consensus enforces consistency across tiles and aspect ratios. args.text: We propose Graph-Edit Contrastive Pretraining (GE-CoP) to address compositional brittleness in image–text models by grounding alignment in explicit relational structure. Concretely, use a family of lightweight adaptation operators—BN-affine updates guided by a self-supervised auxiliary branch and frozen statistics, and visual prompt tuning for frozen backbones—and learn both initialization and update rules to minimize the empirical quantile of loss after a fixed unlabeled adaptation budget. Extend this to an active test-time setting by allocating a small label budget to samples with highest estimated contribution to the tail quantile, and maintain a prompt coreset for recurring domains with quantile-weighted replay to prevent forgetting in the tails. result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised depth completion, where the goal is to recover dense, scale-consistent depth maps from very sparse LiDAR measurements without ground-truth supervision. To enable this decomposed learning despite severe "depth holes" from sparse inputs, the authors introduce a Global Depth Guidance (GDG) module that uses a novel dense-to-sparse attention to propagate dense reference information into sparse targets, and they integrate this into a Decomposed Scale-Consistent Learning (DSCL) framework. Evaluated on KITTI and NYUv2, the method significantly improves RMSE and achieves state-of-the-art results, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining relative depth models with explicit global scale estimation and attentive dense guidance.

args.text: Augmented-Lagrangian Diffusion Control (ALDC) reframes multi-modal controllable generation as a single-trajectory constrained optimization during sampling: at each denoising step, we solve a proximal-style update that balances the diffusion score objective with differentiable control residuals (e.g., edge, segmentation, depth, color histogram, or dense motion), while updating per-control multipliers and penalties across steps. This replaces multi-sampler coupling with one chain whose update adds summed constraint gradients weighted by (λ + ρ·residual), enabling exact, composable constraints with no retraining by defining residuals via frozen control encoders/adapters. We further amortize guidance cost by reusing conditional/unconditional attention and sharing guidance features across timesteps so overhead remains near-constant as controls are added. ALDC targets stronger constraint satisfaction and faster sampling than prior optimization-at-inference or adapter-only methods, and naturally subsumes mask-guided editing and dense motion steering as special cases.

result.text: The paper tackles the limited expressiveness of generalizable implicit neural representations (INRs), which struggle to localize and capture fine-grained, per-coordinate details when a single modulated network must represent many instances. Its key insight is that learning locality-aware latent tokens and selectively aggregating them per coordinate, combined with multi-band (coarse-to-fine) modulation, lets the INR capture both spatially local and spectrally fine details. The method uses a transformer encoder to produce a set of latent tokens that encode local information for an input instance, and a locality-aware INR decoder that aggregates relevant tokens via cross-attention for each coordinate and applies progressive, frequency-band-wise modulation to decode outputs; this selective token aggregation plus multi-band modulation yields stronger spatial and spectral localization and improves downstream tasks like image generation.

result.text: The paper tackles the overlooked variability in benchmarking 3D human pose and shape estimation beyond algorithmic innovations, showing that differences in datasets, backbones, and training strategies can substantially skew reported performance and impede fair comparison. Its key insight is that careful selection and combination of datasets with critical attributes (pose/shape/camera diversity), leveraging backbones pretrained on proximate tasks, and applying appropriate augmentations and loss designs each provide large, complementary gains that rival algorithmic improvements. The authors analyze 31 datasets, benchmark 10 backbone architectures from CNNs to transformers, and systematically ablate training recipes to quantify their impacts, then assemble these findings into strong, reproducible baselines that achieve 47.3 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW and offer practical recommendations and code for fairer future evaluations.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised depth completion, where the goal is to recover dense, scale-consistent depth maps from very sparse LiDAR measurements without ground-truth supervision. The key insight is that absolute (scale-consistent) depth can be decomposed into a scale-agnostic relative depth prediction and a separate global scale estimation, allowing each component to be learned more effectively while leveraging the real-distance information in sparse LiDAR. To enable this decomposed learning despite severe "depth holes" from sparse inputs, the authors introduce a Global Depth Guidance (GDG) module that uses a novel dense-to-sparse attention to propagate dense reference information into sparse targets, and they integrate this into a Decomposed Scale-Consistent Learning (DSCL) framework. Evaluated on KITTI and NYUv2, the method significantly improves RMSE and achieves state-of-the-art results, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining relative depth models with explicit global scale estimation and attentive dense guidance.

result.text: The paper addresses safe constrained reinforcement learning: how to learn policies that maximize reward while satisfying constraints (e.g., safety or fairness). The key insight is to split each policy update into an unconstrained improvement step followed by a projection that explicitly enforces constraints, which yields provable bounds on reward improvement and constraint violation per update. The proposed method, Projection-Based Constrained Policy Optimization (PCPO), implements this two-step procedure and analyzes convergence when projecting under either L2 norm or KL divergence; experiments on control tasks show substantially reduced constraint violations and higher rewards compared to prior methods.

result.text: We propose Graph-Edit Contrastive Pretraining (GE-CoP) to address compositional brittleness in image–text models by grounding alignment in explicit relational structure. For each image–caption pair we parse the caption into a scene graph, generate counterfactual negatives via minimal graph edits (attribute swaps, relation inversions, entity substitutions expanded with knowledge-graph synonyms), and paraphrase them with an LLM to remove lexical artifacts; training uses a graph-edit-distance–weighted contrastive objective that enforces larger margins for more distant edits and a group-wise positive term that pulls together examples sharing a subgraph. We co-train a lightweight scene-graph head with cycle-consistency between text-derived and image-derived graphs to avoid reliance on perfect external parsers, and stabilize learning with a momentum teacher. This unifies hard, structure-aware negatives with structured priors and yields relation- and order-sensitive representations expected to improve ARO/SugarCrepe and relation-centric retrieval without hurting general CLIP transfer.

result.text: The paper tackles hybrid-order community detection, aiming to overcome limitations of purely lower-order (node/edge) and higher-order (motif/hypergraph) methods—specifically hypergraph fragmentation and corruption of original edge structure when adding edges. The key insight is to jointly preserve and exploit both lower- and higher-order connectivity by building a micro-unit connection network that encodes small “micro-units” capturing local motif and edge patterns without indiscriminately adding edges. The method defines a Micro-unit Modularity (MuMod) objective to partition this micro-unit network into micro-unit groups and then maps those groups back to produce overlapping communities in the original graph; experiments on five real datasets show MuMod outperforms twelve baselines.

The paper tackles text-driven image editing, where small prompt changes typically cause wholesale image changes rather than localized edits, and current fixes rely on spatial masks that ignore original content inside the masked region. The key insight is that cross-attention layers in diffusion-based text-to-image models explicitly mediate the mapping between prompt words and spatial layout, so manipulating cross-attention activations can steer which parts of the image respond to which words. The method—Prompt-to-Prompt—operates purely by editing the textual prompt and intervening in cross-attention during denoising (techniques include attention map replacement, attention blending, and attention weighting) to achieve localized word replacement, global specification addition, and fine-grained control over word influence while preserving unrelated image content.

result.text: The paper addresses whether plain, non-hierarchical vision transformers—designed without pose-specific domain knowledge—can serve as simple, scalable, and effective backbones for human pose estimation. The key insight is that such transformers, paired with a lightweight decoder, already possess the capacity, parallelism, and flexibility to outperform specialized architectures when scaled and properly trained, and that knowledge from large models can be efficiently transferred to smaller ones via a lightweight token mechanism. The method, called ViTPose, uses a vanilla ViT to extract instance-level features and a simple decoder to predict keypoints, explores scaling from ~100M to 1B parameters, evaluates different attention types, resolutions, and training/finetuning strategies, and demonstrates knowledge transfer through a dedicated knowledge token. Experiments on MS COCO show that the basic ViTPose beats representative baselines and the largest variant establishes a new state-of-the-art.

result.text: The paper addresses efficient training of N:M structured sparsity—where at most N out of every M consecutive weights are nonzero—without costly pretraining or dense-gradient overhead. Its key insight is to view N:M sparsity as a finite combinatorial selection problem over C(M,N) possible N-sized combinations per M-block and to learn which combinations are best via differentiable scores rather than exhaustively searching. The method divides each M-block into all combination subsets, assigns each subset a learnable score that is jointly optimized with its associated weights, and progressively prunes low-scored subsets during standard training, yielding an efficient divide-and-conquer procedure that models relative importance among combinations and outperforms prior N:M pruning approaches.

args.text: Plug-and-Play denoisers often see iterates that mismatch their training degradation; SNORE addresses this with Gaussian re-noising, and DPnP relies on stochastic diffusion priors. I propose operator-aware cold re-noising: before each denoising step, apply a deterministic corruption chain, trained in the cold-diffusion style, that mirrors the forward operator’s blur/aliasing/masking so the denoiser always inverts the task-aligned degradation. We instantiate the denoiser as a learned proximal network and embed it in PnP-PGD/ADMM, preserving nonconvex proximal convergence while annealing the corruption strength with the data-fidelity residual. This yields deterministic, faster-converging reconstructions with fewer hallucinations in structured inverse problems such as MRI, CT, and deblurring.

result.text: The paper tackles domain generalization under distribution shift, where training data come from multiple known domains but models must handle unseen test-time shifts; instead of assuming a single invariant model will generalize, it targets scenarios where unlabeled test points can be used for adaptation. The key insight is to optimize models not for static robustness but for their ability to adapt: train them to perform effective unsupervised test-time adaptation by simulating domain shifts during training so they learn adaptation procedures that transfer. Methodologically, the authors introduce Adaptive Risk Minimization (ARM), a framework that explicitly trains models to adapt on held-out domains by minimizing expected post-adaptation risk—implementing concrete algorithms that learn adaptation rules or parameterizations and evaluating them on image classification benchmarks, where ARM yields consistent 1–4% accuracy improvements over prior robustness and invariance approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses image-guided depth completion, where sparse depth measurements and an RGB image must be fused to produce a dense depth map, and it targets limitations of existing spatial propagation networks (SPNs) such as fixed affinities and iterative over-smoothing. The key insight is to replace fixed, shared affinities with iteration-specific, attention-driven affinities that are efficiently generated by decoupling neighborhoods by distance and recursively producing independent attention maps, combined with a diffusion suppression (DS) operation to halt excessive smoothing once convergence is reached. The proposed Dynamic Spatial Propagation Network (DySPN) implements a non-linear propagation model that refines distance-partitioned neighbor groups into adaptive affinity matrices via dynamic attention, uses DS to converge earlier and avoid blur, and offers three lightweight variants that reduce neighbor/attention counts to cut computation while maintaining accuracy. Empirically, DySPN requires fewer propagation iterations and achieves state-of-the-art results on KITTI depth completion and strong performance on NYU Depth v2.

result.text: The paper tackles safe exploration in episodic constrained Markov decision processes, asking whether one can obtain near-optimal reward regret while eliminating or sharply limiting constraint violations. Its key insight is that combining optimism for reward with pessimism for constraints—leveraging a known strictly safe baseline when available or conservatively estimating constraint costs otherwise—lets an agent explore without incurring growing safety breaches. Concretely, when a strictly safe policy is known the authors design an optimistic-pessimistic algorithm that confines constraint violation to zero with high probability while maintaining Õ(√K) reward regret; when no safe policy is known but one exists, they give a primal–dual method that uses optimistic primal estimates and pessimistic dual updates to guarantee only bounded constraint violation with high probability alongside Õ(√K) regret.

result.text: Uni-ControlNet addresses the limitation of text-to-image diffusion models in expressing and obeying detailed, multi-modal constraints by enabling flexible, composable control beyond text (e.g., edge maps, depth, segmentation, CLIP embeddings) within a single model. The key insight is that a small set of dedicated, modular adapters can be fine-tuned on top of frozen pre-trained diffusion backbones to absorb diverse local and global controls while keeping parameter and computational costs low; by designing adapters that share structure and operate agnostically across control types, the number of additional modules remains constant (two) regardless of how many control signals are used. Method-wise, Uni-ControlNet inserts and fine-tunes two adapter networks into the frozen text-to-image diffusion pipeline to encode and fuse various local and global conditioning signals, enabling composability and simultaneous multi-control generation without training from scratch, and demonstrating improved controllability and image quality in quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

A lightweight encoder learns an implicit degradation representation from the LR input, which conditions both the dynamic filtering in the SR head and the bandwidth of periodic positional encodings so the coordinate-to-pixel predictor adapts its frequency response per region and requested scale. This single model targets robust, continuous-scale SR under unknown degradations, unifying continuous SR and blind SR while reducing artifacts at high magnifications.

result.text: We propose Graph-Edit Contrastive Pretraining (GE-CoP) to address compositional brittleness in image–text models by grounding alignment in explicit relational structure. For each image–caption pair we parse the caption into a scene graph, generate counterfactual negatives via minimal graph edits (attribute swaps, relation inversions, entity substitutions expanded with knowledge-graph synonyms), and paraphrase them with an LLM to remove lexical artifacts; training uses a graph-edit-distance–weighted contrastive objective that enforces larger margins for more distant edits and a group-wise positive term that pulls together examples sharing a subgraph. We co-train a lightweight scene-graph head with cycle-consistency between text-derived and image-derived graphs to avoid reliance on perfect external parsers, and stabilize learning with a momentum teacher. This unifies hard, structure-aware negatives with structured priors and yields relation- and order-sensitive representations expected to improve ARO/SugarCrepe and relation-centric retrieval without hurting general CLIP transfer.

result.text: The paper tackles lightweight image super-resolution by designing attention mechanisms tailored to SR’s pixel-level needs rather than borrowing patch-based Transformer designs from high-level vision. Motivated by Local Attribution Maps that reveal a hierarchical importance pattern—highly important pixels concentrated in a fine local area and less important cues dispersed coarsely across the image—the authors propose a hybrid attention block: a Global Pixel Access (GPA) module that cheaply retrieves coarse-context pixels via cross-attention with the most similar patch, an Intra-Patch Self-Attention (IPSA) module to capture long-range dependencies within local patches, and a final spatial convolution to refine the finest details; they further introduce Cascaded Patch Division (CPD) to improve perceptual quality. This coarse-to-fine hierarchical pixel integration yields a lightweight SR network (HPINet) that significantly outperforms prior lightweight methods in both fidelity and perceptual reconstruction.

args.text: Part-Aware Test-Time Volumetric Personalization (PTVP) adapts a SMPL-X–anchored 3D Gaussian human avatar per subject at inference by optimizing only lightweight, per-part latent pose offsets and Gaussian radiance/density scales under self-supervised render-and-compare objectives. We couple Gaussian human avatars with an articulated photometric/silhouette reprojection loss and a self-supervised keypoint head whose outputs are mapped to supervised space via a learned transformer, enabling fast, label-free personalization that sharpens hands and face while preserving global body plausibility from an EHPS foundation prior. To further stabilize fine hand articulation during object interaction, we incorporate contact-aware regularizers: a hand–object contact detector supplies soft constraints that keep fingertips and palmar surfaces on or near detected object surfaces with nonpenetration/slide penalties. Pretrained on large-scale EHPS data for strong priors, PTVP performs short per-subject adaptation from monocular videos and aims to yield crisper detail, fewer interpenetrations, and more stable motion on in-the-wild sequences.

result.text: The paper addresses the performance gap between low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and full fine-tuning of foundation models, asking whether LoRA is being properly optimized. The key insight is that LoRA-based optimization is mathematically equivalent to full fine-tuning with a low-rank gradient, and that this low-rank gradient can be expressed directly from the gradients of LoRA’s two low-rank matrices; therefore, improving LoRA amounts to better approximating the full-fine-tuning gradient via adjustments to those matrix gradients. result.text: The paper tackles safe offline reinforcement learning, where enforcing zero safety violations is critical but difficult because it requires balancing safety, reward maximization, and staying close to offline data. The key insight is that hard safety constraints can be reformulated via reachability analysis as identifying the largest feasible region supported by the dataset, turning the original tri-objective into a feasibility-dependent objective that maximizes reward inside the feasible region and minimizes risk outside it. Building on this, the authors propose FISOR (FeasIbility-guided Safe Offline RL), which decouples constraint adherence, reward optimization, and behavior regularization into three processes and shows the optimal policy takes the form of a weighted behavior cloning solution. result.text: The paper addresses safe reinforcement learning in stochastic environments, aiming to guarantee persistent, state-wise safety while avoiding overly conservative behavior and handling cases where completely safe policies may not exist. Its key insight is to frame safety via an iterative reachability estimation that distinguishes a feasible set of states where violation-free policies exist and, outside that set, directs optimization toward behaviors that minimize cumulative discounted violations and reach the feasible set when possible. We propose Graph-Edit Contrastive Pretraining (GE-CoP) to address compositional brittleness in image–text models by grounding alignment in explicit relational structure. args.text: We propose a unified, budget-aware scheduler that jointly optimizes reasoning search and speculative decoding to maximize task accuracy under a fixed latency constraint. At each step, a learned controller allocates compute between expanding value-guided reasoning branches and reshaping the drafting process (e.g., adjusting non-autoregressive draft length, candidate width, and block verification cadence) based on online signals like draft acceptance rate, verification cost predictors, and value uncertainty. We formalize this as a contextual bandit that minimizes regret versus an oracle allocator and train it in a simulator seeded with hardware/latency models; at runtime it adapts per-query to shifting bottlenecks (KV costs, acceptance drift) while preserving exact sampling where required. Preliminary expectation is that small models with this scheduler match or surpass larger models and static policies on math and long-context benchmarks with lower end-to-end latency.

result.text: ControlRouter is a training-free arbitration plugin for composable multi-modal control in text-to-image diffusion. Rather than naively summing controls, it solves at each sampling step a small per-pixel simplex-constrained weighting of control features or guidance gradients that minimizes control-specific differentiable consistency losses (e.g., edge distance, depth RMSE, mask IoU) while preserving text semantics via cross-attention masks. The resulting weights gate adapter/ControlNet injections and are temporally smoothed across steps, while a MultiDiffusion-style consensus enforces consistency across tiles and aspect ratios. This yields sharper, more faithful structure–style compositions and graceful degradation when controls disagree, without retraining the backbone or adapters.

result.text: The paper addresses the rigidity of neural image compression (NIC), where different rate-distortion (R-D) operating points typically require separate encoder-decoder pairs or inflexible conditional schemes, limiting practical deployment and adaptability. Its key insight is that variable bitrate and flexible coding goals can be achieved at inference time by "editing" a single latent code via semi-amortized optimization and adaptive quantization, rather than baking rate control into the network during training. The method performs semi-amortized inference to iteratively refine the latent representation for a given R-D target, applies adaptive, learnable quantization to adjust bitrate and distortion trade-offs, and thus enables variable-rate coding, region-of-interest (ROI) prioritization, and multi-distortion objectives with a single decoder. Experimental results demonstrate that this code-editing approach outperforms prior variable-rate NIC methods while providing much greater flexibility.

args.text: We tackle the residual verification bottleneck in lossless speculative decoding: even with improved drafting and joint block checks, the target model frequently runs full forward passes to accept drafts, which dominates latency in long-context, large-batch regimes. Our key insight is Certified Partial Verification (CPV): replace many full verifications with certified partial ones that propagate tight, precomputed layer-wise Lipschitz bounds and Jacobian–vector products to produce upper/lower bounds on target logits for a drafted block; when these bounds certify that the block-verification/optimal-transport acceptance would succeed, we accept without executing the remaining layers, else we fall back to exact verification. CPV preserves the exact-sample guarantee because acceptance occurs only under formal certificates, and when combined with joint block verification and KV-optimized serving it reduces target invocations on “easy” proposals to yield additional end-to-end speedups. A practical design amortizes bound computation across the batch and reuses cached per-prompt sensitivities, making CPV complementary to current block-verification and MagicDec-style systems.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of image compression by proposing an alternative to traditional pixel-based or learned-codebook methods that instead represents an image implicitly. The key insight is that overfitting a small multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to map continuous pixel coordinates to RGB values produces a compact, continuous representation whose learned weights encode the image and can be quantized to form a compressed code; this implicit neural representation can outperform JPEG at low bitrates even without entropy coding. The method fits an MLP per image, quantizes and stores the network weights as the compressed file, and reconstructs the image by evaluating the MLP at each pixel, and the paper empirically demonstrates competitive low-rate performance and highlights desirable properties (e.g., continuous resolution and simplicity) suggesting potential for further development.

args.text: Amortized Single-Sample Prompting (ASP) for CTTA: instead of maintaining per-domain prompt coresets, train a conditional hypernetwork that maps a single test image to a visual prompt for a frozen backbone, enabling per-sample adaptation with a single forward pass. For nonstationary streams, we attach a tiny key–value memory of low-rank adapters for the prompt generator, updated online from short windows and retrieved by similarity, to rapidly snap back on revisits without overwriting the base. This combines the efficiency of prompt CTTA with the flexibility of single-sample adaptation and yields faster, lower-compute alignment than prompt coresets under brief, heterogeneous shifts.

Train the generative mapper and uncertainty head purely from passive roaming video (bootstrapping maps via self-supervised SLAM) so no simulator RL is needed, and update the prior online as evidence accrues. args.text: We propose Lagrange-guided diffusion policies for safe RL that integrate conservative primal–dual control into the sampling process to achieve zero constraint violations while optimizing reward. The policy is a budget-conditioned diffusion generator whose score is guided by dual-weighted safety gradients; dual variables follow conservative updates to stabilize and strictly enforce constraints. We initialize and mask the sampler with an offline feasibility map learned via reachability from fixed data, and use efficient single-/few-step denoising so the policy can project to the feasible set in real time and adapt to dynamic safety budgets. This unifies diffusion planning, projection-based enforcement, and conservative dual control to enable near-optimal performance with provable zero violations in offline deployment and safe online fine-tuning.

args.text: We propose Tree-Coupled Block Verification (TCBV), where the speculator drafts a shallow prefix tree over the next H steps by selecting m OT-coupled candidates per position (sharing probability mass across branches) rather than a single linear block. The target performs a single joint verification pass over this tree by batching logits on shared prefixes and applying a tree-structured maximal-coupling test to select the longest fully accepted path, falling back by pruning when necessary; this preserves exact sampling, strictly dominates token-wise checks, and reduces to standard block verification when m=1. A horizontal scheduler allocates drafting effort to depths/nodes with high entropy or low coupling scores while a vertical, non‑autoregressive drafter proposes nodes in parallel, reducing wasted compute. Compared to flat block speculation, TCBV increases expected accepted tokens per iteration in ambiguous next-token regimes and lowers wall-clock time, with further gains when the draft model is online-adapted to the live query distribution.

result.text: The paper addresses understanding why Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is so effective for parameter-efficient fine-tuning by formally analyzing its expressive power: specifically, what class of target models can be represented by adding low-rank adapters to a pre-trained network. The key insight is that LoRA’s capacity is governed by a simple rank threshold that depends on the source model’s width and the relative depths of source and target networks, and that sufficiently large but still low-rank adapters suffice to emulate smaller target models exactly. Methodologically, the authors prove constructive representation theorems for fully connected networks—showing LoRA can adapt any model f to any smaller target \overline{f} when LoRA rank ≥ (width of f) × (depth of \overline{f} / depth of f) and provide bounds on approximation error below this threshold—and extend the analysis to Transformers, proving rank-(embedding size/2) adapters can realize any same-size target model.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of learning object-centric world models that can maintain coherent belief states in partially observable environments, where existing approaches fail to track objects through occlusion and uncertainty. The key insight is to combine Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) inference with object-centric representations and an inductive bias for object permanence, yielding multi-hypothesis, particle-based beliefs that preserve and reason about unseen object states. The method, Structured World Belief (SWB), integrates SMC to produce multiple object-centric scene hypotheses, a dynamics model that enforces object permanence to maintain state through long invisibility, and flexible spatial attention that lets object slots attend anywhere in the image; experiments show SWB improves filtering, generation, reinforcement learning, planning, and supervised reasoning under partial observability.

The paper addresses the problem that existing vision-language compositionality benchmarks are heavily biased and therefore "hackable"—so much so that models that ignore images can outperform state-of-the-art systems when distinguishing correct captions from compositional distractors. The key insight is that prior benchmarks relied on brittle, rule-based negative generation that leaves predictable statistical cues, and that using large language models plus an adversarial refinement loop can produce fluent, semantically plausible hard negatives that remove these artifacts. The authors introduce SugarCrepe, a new benchmark built by prompting LLMs to generate candidate distractors and then iteratively filtering and adversarially refining them to minimize dataset biases, and they show via re-evaluation that many claimed gains from compositionality methods were overstated. They release the benchmark and evaluation code to enable more robust progress on vision-language compositionality.

The key insight is that transformers trained long enough can internally represent the in-context empirical conditional distribution of the next symbol, allowing low test loss even as k increases, and that this representation can be achieved with surprisingly shallow networks. Concretely, use a family of lightweight adaptation operators—BN-affine updates guided by a self-supervised auxiliary branch and frozen statistics, and visual prompt tuning for frozen backbones—and learn both initialization and update rules to minimize the empirical quantile of loss after a fixed unlabeled adaptation budget. result.text: The paper tackles offline reinforcement learning’s core dilemma of improving beyond the behavior policy while avoiding distributional shift from evaluating out-of-distribution actions. The key insight is to never directly query unseen actions but instead treat the state value as a random variable induced by dataset actions and use a state-conditional upper expectile of that distribution to implicitly approximate the value of the best actions, thereby leveraging function approximation to generalize without evaluating OOD actions. The method, Implicit Q-Learning (IQL), alternates between fitting this upper-expectile value function and backing it up into a Q-function, and then derives a policy via advantage-weighted behavioral cloning. IQL attains state-of-the-art performance on the D4RL offline RL benchmark and transfers effectively to online fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of enforcing strict formal constraints on LLM outputs without hurting accuracy or slowing generation, noting that existing constrained decoding methods often misalign with subword vocabularies and introduce runtime overhead or degraded task performance. Its key insight is that constraints must be enforced in a fully subword-aligned way and that combining subword alignment with precomputation and speculative decoding can eliminate overhead and preserve model accuracy. The authors introduce DOMINO, a decoding algorithm that aligns external constraints to the model’s subword units, precomputes constraint-related structures, and uses speculative decoding to validate long unconstrained token proposals quickly; this yields constraint-compliant generation with negligible cost and in some cases nearly 2× speedup versus unconstrained decoding while outperforming prior constrained-decode methods.

Consensus-Control Diffusion: a training-free mechanism that, at each denoising step, unrolls a few iterations of a small consensus optimization (ADMM-style) to reconcile the base denoiser with multiple heterogeneous controls (edges/depth/segmentation/color/flow/text regions). Each control contributes either a differentiable guidance loss (e.g., optical-flow or mask consistency) or a latent proposal from a lightweight adapter; the consensus update blends these via spatially varying weights estimated from per-control uncertainty derived from score variance between conditional/unconditional and a degraded "bad-guide" ensemble. This yields per-pixel, per-timestep allocation of a control budget—structure-heavy pixels lean on visual controls while style/background lean on text—while multi-crop/tiling proposals are fused in the same consensus to support large canvases. The approach preserves diversity relative to strong CFG, improves constraint satisfaction over naive guidance, and remains modular and composable across new control types without retraining.

args.text: I propose nullspace-aware cold re-noising for PnP: at each iteration, first project the estimate to the data-consistent affine set, decompose it into measurement-space and nullspace components, then apply a deterministic operator-conditioned cold corruption only in the nullspace (e.g., blur, masking, or spectral shrinkage aligned to A’s singular spectrum) before denoising with a learned proximal network trained under the same nullspace-only corruption. This preserves data consistency while reinstating diffusion-like regularization exactly along directions the likelihood cannot constrain, reducing hallucinations and improving stability. Because the denoiser is an exact proximal map and the nullspace corruption is nonexpansive, the composite update fits the nonconvex proximal-gradient theory, and we adapt corruption strength via a discrepancy principle tied to the residual. Instantiations for MRI (k-space line masking restricted to unmeasured coils/lines) and CT (angular subsampling within unmeasured views) accelerate convergence and improve perceptual fidelity relative to Gaussian re-noising.

The key insight is that adding a tiny, constant-sized recurrent cache that synthesizes and preserves summarized recurrence can complement eviction-based caches so that no token is truly unrecoverable, allowing the model to query approximate historical information without storing all KV pairs. The method, called LESS, integrates a nearly-free fixed-size recurrent cache with standard eviction or pruning strategies: during decoding LESS maintains and updates a compact summary representation of past states while evicted full KV entries remain removable, enabling the decoder to reconstruct or approximate older context when needed. Experiments show LESS substantially narrows (and sometimes closes) the performance gap with full caching across diverse tasks while drastically reducing memory use.

We decompose each control (edges, depth, masks, flow, text attention maps) into multiscale bands (e.g., Laplacian/steerable pyramid) and apply a noise-level–conditioned schedule that emphasizes low frequencies early and high frequencies late, matching the diffusion sampler’s intrinsic frequency progression. Practically, existing adapter/guidance injections or control losses are bandpass-filtered and weighted per band at each step, with a small simplex-constrained budget allocator (as in ControlRouter) to arbitrate between controls; MultiDiffusion crops use band-consistent consensus. This training-free wrapper reduces conflicts and oversmoothing in multi-control composition and yields sharper structure with cleaner textures versus naive summation or static weights.

The method, TinyTrain, implements this by dynamically selecting which layers and channels to update during training based on data-driven importance and device-aware constraints, thereby minimizing backward-pass memory and computation while explicitly coping with few-shot data; experiments show substantial accuracy gains over full fine-tuning and large reductions in memory, compute, time, and energy, enabling training within MCU-grade (≈1 MB) envelopes.

This paper introduces MultiON, a benchmark that extends ObjectGoal navigation to sequences of episode-specific target objects in photorealistic 3D environments to study how map-like memory supports navigation under partial observability. The key insight is that increasingly complex multi-object navigation tasks reveal distinct capabilities and failures of memory representations—performance falls sharply as task complexity grows, and surprisingly simple semantic map representations can outperform more complex learned image-feature map agents. The authors construct the MultiON task suite, evaluate a range of agents (including reactive baselines, learned neural-map agents, semantic-map agents, and oracle-map upper bounds) across task difficulty, and analyze results to show both the benefits of explicit semantic mapping and substantial remaining gaps even for oracle maps, highlighting opportunities for improved map-based training and planning.

args.text: Reachability-Guided Contrastive Diffusion for Safe Offline RL (ReaGCD): learn from offline data a reachability-based feasible-state estimator and budget-conditioned cost-to-go, then train a diffusion policy on dataset actions together with a CEP-style contrastive energy that provides exact intermediate guidance combining (i) reward, (ii) in-sample distribution-ratio guidance, and (iii) a safety energy enforcing feasibility and real-time budgets. During sampling, guidance keeps trajectories in-distribution and within the feasible set; when initialized outside it, the sampler is biased toward shortest-feasible return paths under the specified budget. To preserve generalization without OOD overestimation, we mildly train pseudo-Q targets on sampled candidate OOD actions and perform a final candidate selection that enforces feasibility/budget constraints. This unifies reachability guarantees with exact energy-guided diffusion and DICE-based in-sample correction, targeting zero violations when a feasible policy exists and minimal discounted violations otherwise while improving return–safety trade-offs in the purely offline setting.

result.text: We propose Graph-Edit Contrastive Pretraining (GE-CoP) to address compositional brittleness in image–text models by grounding alignment in explicit relational structure. For each image–caption pair we parse the caption into a scene graph, generate counterfactual negatives via minimal graph edits (attribute swaps, relation inversions, entity substitutions expanded with knowledge-graph synonyms), and paraphrase them with an LLM to remove lexical artifacts; training uses a graph-edit-distance–weighted contrastive objective that enforces larger margins for more distant edits and a group-wise positive term that pulls together examples sharing a subgraph. We co-train a lightweight scene-graph head with cycle-consistency between text-derived and image-derived graphs to avoid reliance on perfect external parsers, and stabilize learning with a momentum teacher. This unifies hard, structure-aware negatives with structured priors and yields relation- and order-sensitive representations expected to improve ARO/SugarCrepe and relation-centric retrieval without hurting general CLIP transfer.
